doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

chapter: Rahsaan Roland Kirk and the conch shell
title: Rahsaan introduces the conch shell; Turré gets his first one in 1970
summary: Rahsaan plays a shell for loud, rude patrons at a club and brings peace to the room.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Did he play a role in your exploration of the conch shell?

Yeah. Because he introduced me to it in person. I’d seen a few people in the movies go woooh, you know. But he had a shell. He had all kinds of things that he made sounds with you know. And he had a shell and he had it down at the side and the saxophones were on the stand and all that. Three nights went by and he didn’t play it and it was just sitting there. And I said, I said, “Rahsaan, the shell there, are you going to play that?” And he said, “I’ll play it when the time is right.” Okay. Sure. As fate would have it, the next night, you know we’re in the club. Anybody can walk in the club, it’s open to the public. You get all kinds of crazy people. Well this couple came in and sat right in the front table, right in front of the bandstand and proceeded to get drunk as can be, talking loud, oblivious to the music, it was rude. And you know Rahsaan kept playing. Then he wanted to play a ballad. It was a quiet thing. And they’re just talking loud, and the woman said, “Man I told you to take out the garbage.” And the guy said, “I did.” She said, “No you didn’t, you left it by the side of the car there.” And they’re going back and forth and so Rahsaan gets out the shell. Now Rahsaan is the kind of circular breathing and that whole publicity stunt with Kenny G, you know and I know that was a farce, and I put that on the record too. If Rahsaan had been alive he would have showed up and

blown him away. But anyway Rahsaan took the shell and, with circular breathing [vocalizes], but he yelled it for like five minutes, which is a long time you know. And these people, they finally realized something was going on, this sound. And they stopped talking and went [gasps] and when they did that everybody in the club goes yaaay. You know. And then there was silence. Then there was silence and Rahsaan went into a ballad with the tenor saxophone, real breathy like a Ben Webster kind of vibe. [scats]. You know it was beautiful man. But what the sound of the shell did was it brought peace. It brought another kind of energy to the air. It’s different than a man-made brass instrument. It’s not metal. It was alive once. But it is the roots of brass instruments. I was reading within the last year there was an article I read about some archaeologists found a shell instrument that was 17 thousand years old. So that’s before written history. Before people were playing instruments. I use the same embouchure.

Rahsaan just played the one note and I loved it. So I said after the gig was over and we were packing up, I said, “Man could I try that?” And he said, “Yeah, go ahead.” And I blew on it and I said, “Oh man, I’ve got to get one of these.” So my mom was going on vacation a couple of months later. She went to Hawaii. And I asked her, “If you see a shell instrument pick one up for me.” And she did. And I still play it to this day. And that was 1970 I got my first shell.
